mission.title: What Is Meant Without Being Said

theory.title: Conversational implicature and cooperative expectations
theory.explanation: An implicature is meaning inferred in context rather than directly encoded. Grice's conversational maxims are often grouped as Quantity (enough information), Quality (truthfulness and evidence), Relation (relevance) and Manner (clarity). Speakers may observe, infringe or deliberately flout these expectations. A flout can invite irony, understatement or indirect criticism. Scalar expressions such as some often suggest not all, but that inference can be cancelled. Implicatures are defeasible: a different context can support a different interpretation.
theory.tip: Write down the literal commitment first. Then identify the expectation that seems unmet and test at least one alternative inference.

patterns.label: Quantity
patterns.pattern: Give neither too little nor more than the context requires.
examples: “Some attended” may suggest that not everyone attended.

patterns.label: Quality
patterns.pattern: Do not present as true what you believe to be false or lack evidence for.
examples: Obvious exaggeration can signal irony rather than literal assertion.

patterns.label: Relation
patterns.pattern: Make your contribution relevant to the current exchange.
examples: “The window is open” may indirectly request that someone close it.

patterns.label: Manner
examples: An unusually vague answer may signal reluctance to commit.

content.passage:
At the end of a lengthy presentation, the chair asked whether the proposal had attracted “substantial support”. The analyst replied that “a number of colleagues had expressed interest”. The answer was accurate, but conspicuously less direct than the question. Listeners inferred that support was limited, although the analyst had not said so explicitly.

Such inferences are not arbitrary. In ordinary conversation, speakers are generally expected to provide relevant, sufficiently informative and truthful contributions, expressed with reasonable clarity. When an answer appears to fall short of these expectations, hearers look for a reason. Perhaps the analyst wished to avoid overstating the evidence; perhaps the choice of wording was intended to signal reservations. The context makes the latter plausible, but does not make it certain.

The distinction between an implicature and an entailment is therefore essential. An implicature can often be cancelled without contradiction: “A number of colleagues expressed interest—in fact, almost everyone did.” A careful interpreter asks what the utterance literally commits the speaker to, what it invites the audience to infer, and what further evidence would justify that inference.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between literal meaning and conversational implicature.
items.modelAnswer: Literal meaning is encoded by the words and structure; conversational implicature is inferred from context and assumptions about how people normally communicate.

items.prompt: Analyse what might be implied by “That is an interesting suggestion” in a sceptical discussion.
items.modelAnswer: It may be genuine interest, polite reservation or indirect disagreement; intonation, follow-up and prior context help distinguish these readings.

items.prompt: Describe how a speaker can flout a conversational maxim without simply communicating badly.
items.modelAnswer: A speaker may visibly depart from an expectation so that the listener searches for an additional, often figurative or ironic, meaning.

items.prompt: Give an example of an implicature that can be cancelled and explain why.
items.modelAnswer: “Some students passed—in fact, all did” cancels the likely inference that not all passed without contradicting the literal meaning of some.

items.prompt: Discuss whether indirectness is always a sign of politeness.
items.modelAnswer: Indirectness can soften disagreement, but it can also obscure responsibility, create ambiguity or be used strategically; context and power relations matter.

items.prompt: Interpret “I wouldn't call it a triumph” after a disappointing launch.
items.modelAnswer: The speaker avoids a direct negative label but clearly signals that the launch fell short of success.

items.prompt: Explain how irony relies on a gap between literal wording and intended meaning.
items.modelAnswer: Irony invites the listener to notice a mismatch between the literal evaluation and contextual evidence, tone or shared assumptions.

items.prompt: How would you respond if someone treated an implicature as undeniable proof?
items.modelAnswer: I would acknowledge that the inference is plausible while distinguishing it from what the speaker explicitly committed themselves to.

items.prompt: Compare a direct refusal with an indirect refusal in a professional setting.
items.modelAnswer: A direct refusal is unambiguous and efficient; an indirect one may preserve rapport but risks leaving the decision unclear.

items.prompt: Give two plausible readings of “We will bear that in mind” and explain what would disambiguate them.
items.modelAnswer: It may signal genuine consideration or polite dismissal; subsequent action, tone and the speaker's role provide relevant evidence.

content.audioTranscript: Asked whether the trial had been a success, the researcher said that the results were encouraging in several respects. She added that the sample was relatively small and that further work would be needed before any firm claims could be made. Her answer was cautiously positive, but it stopped short of endorsing the intervention.
